results.result: TPE-FLIM can distinguish M1 and M2 macrophages in vitro based on distinct fluorescence lifetime parameters and morphological features. M1 macrophages (n=21) showed significantly shorter fluorescence decay times (τm=479±106 ps) compared to M2 macrophages (n=27, τm=1,185±170 ps, p<0.05), with M1 cells exhibiting numerous bright spots, less visible borders, and higher TPE-AF intensity, while M2 cells displayed distinct borders with filopodia.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C51 provide converging evidence from in vitro experiments with appropriate sample sizes (n=21 M1, n=27 M2), statistical testing (p<0.05), and multiple distinguishing parameters (τ1, τ2, τm, morphology). The morphological observations are supported by imaging data (Figure 2), and both monocyte-derived and isolated dermal macrophages show consistent patterns.

results.result: Human dermal macrophages isolated from periocular skin segregate into two groups based on TPE-FLIM parameters that correspond to M1 and M2 phenotypes. Group 1 (n=34) showed stronger TPE-AF intensity (≈3000±500 photons/mW) and shorter lifetimes similar to M1 macrophages, while group 2 (n=28) exhibited weaker intensity (≈800±200 photons/mW) and longer lifetimes similar to M2 macrophages, with significant size differences (10.9±0.6 µm vs 9.8±1.2 µm, p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C61 demonstrate that dermal macrophages isolated from tissue exhibit TPE-FLIM signatures matching those of monocyte-derived M1/M2 macrophages. The data include adequate sample sizes (n=34, n=28), statistical significance testing, and multiple distinguishing parameters. This validates the in vitro findings in a more physiologically relevant context.

results.result: M1 and M2 macrophages can be distinguished from other dermal cells (mast cells, neutrophils, fibroblasts, dendritic cells) by distinct TPE-FLIM parameters in addition to morphological features. Macrophages exhibited higher fluorescence intensity than other dermal cells, were larger than mast cells, had different morphology from neutrophils and fibroblasts, and showed vacuole structures linked to their TPE-FLIM parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C120-C125 establish that macrophages have unique TPE-FLIM signatures compared to other dermal cell types. The comparative data in Table 1 shows distinct parameter ranges for each cell type, and morphological differences provide additional distinguishing features. This is essential for validating the specificity of the method.

results.result: TPE-FLIM identification of M1 and M2 macrophages in human skin biopsies was validated by immunohistochemistry. In 13 cryo-sections, cells with short τm and high TPE-AF intensity were confirmed as M1 macrophages by CD68 staining (8/9 TPE-FLIM identified cells were CD68+), while cells with longer τm and lower intensity were confirmed as M2 macrophages by CD163 staining (12/14 TPE-FLIM identified cells were CD163+).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C76, C126, and C131 provide critical validation using an independent gold-standard method (immunohistochemistry). The concordance rates are high (89% for M1, 86% for M2), and importantly, all antibody-positive cells showed the expected TPE-FLIM signatures, demonstrating both sensitivity and specificity of the method ex vivo.

results.result: TPE-FLIM successfully visualized M1 (n=35) and M2 (n=25) macrophages in vivo in the skin of 25 healthy individuals. Macrophages were located in the papillary and reticular dermis at >80 µm depth with a density of >100 cells/mm². M1 macrophages showed three morphological variants (flat spindle-shaped, slightly dendritic, or large intervascular), while M2 macrophages were round and moderately dendritic with higher TPE-AF intensity than ECM.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83, C87, C103, and C134 demonstrate successful translation of the method to in vivo human imaging. The study includes adequate sample size (25 subjects), identifies sufficient cells for analysis (35 M1, 25 M2), and shows consistency with in vitro and ex vivo findings. The TPE-FLIM parameters of in vivo M1 macrophages matched those from other conditions, validating the approach.

results.result: A machine learning decision tree classifier was developed to automatically identify M1 and M2 macrophages based on TPE-FLIM parameters. The algorithm achieved high performance: ground truth validation showed 0.95±0.05 sensitivity and 0.97±0.06 specificity; M1 macrophage classification achieved 0.88±0.04 sensitivity and 0.89±0.03 specificity; M2 macrophage classification achieved 0.82±0.03 sensitivity and 0.90±0.03 specificity. Five-fold cross-validation yielded a mean score of 0.90.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C97-C102, C105, C170, and C175 describe a well-validated machine learning approach. The classifier uses appropriate features (TPE-FLIM parameters), includes proper validation (cross-validation, train-test splits repeated 10,000 times), and achieves good performance metrics. The methodology addresses overfitting concerns and demonstrates reproducibility.

results.result: TPE-FLIM can potentially distinguish phagocytosing M1 macrophages from resting macrophages in vivo. Phagocytosing M1 macrophages are characterized by increased cell size (≈25 µm), enhanced vacuolization, shorter fluorescence lifetimes, and acidification with ROS production. Of 37 dermal M1 macrophages analyzed in vivo, 2 showed possible phagocytosis activity, both located in the reticular dermis below 100 µm depth.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96, C104, and C158-C160 describe characteristics of phagocytosing macrophages supported by citations, but the in vivo identification is based on only 2 cells out of 37 analyzed. While the cited literature supports the expected features of phagocytosing cells, the extremely small sample size (n=2) and lack of independent validation (e.g., confirmation of actual phagocytosis) make this finding preliminary and requiring further validation.

results.result: M2 macrophages in vivo exhibited longer mean fluorescence lifetime τm compared to in vitro and ex vivo measurements, though τ1 and τ2 values were consistent with in vitro PBMC-derived monocytes. This difference is attributed to environmental influences including missing growth factors, cytokines, and elevated nutrient levels in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 and C135-C137 acknowledge and explain systematic differences between in vivo and in vitro measurements. The interpretation is supported by citations to relevant literature on microenvironment effects. The consistency of some parameters (τ1, τ2) with in vitro measurements while others differ (τm) suggests biological rather than technical artifacts.

results.result: TPE-FLIM parameters remained stable over extended measurement periods: up to 1 hour for in vitro macrophages isolated from periocular skin and up to 30 minutes for in vivo macrophages in human skin. No unprompted changes in fluorescence lifetime or intensity were observed when laser power was kept below levels that induce photoproducts or photobleaching.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C88, and C150-C151 demonstrate temporal stability of the measurements, which is critical for validating that observed signals reflect biological properties rather than measurement artifacts. The time-course data (Figures 2—figure supplement 4, 4—figure supplements 2-3) support these claims with appropriate controls for laser-induced damage.

results.result: The TPE-FLIM differences between M1 and M2 macrophages are explained by distinct metabolic profiles. M1 macrophages show higher TPE-AF intensity indicating metabolic stress, rely on glycolysis and NADH oxidase with ROS production (fluorescence lifetimes <250 ps), and exhibit mitochondrial fission. M2 macrophages rely on oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation with mitochondrial fusion, resulting in longer fluorescence lifetimes (τ2) due to higher ratios of bound to free NAD(P)H.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C113 and C115-C116 provide mechanistic interpretation of the TPE-FLIM observations, well-supported by citations to established literature on macrophage metabolism and NAD(P)H fluorescence properties. The interpretation is consistent with known metabolic differences between M1 and M2 phenotypes and explains the observed fluorescence lifetime patterns.

results.result: Background on macrophage biology: Macrophages are immune effector cells that promote (M1) or inhibit (M2) inflammation. Skin macrophages originate from circulating monocytes, are located in the papillary and reticular dermis near blood vessels, and have been known for >30 years to be abundant and heterogeneous. M1 macrophages are activated by infection, IFN-γ, LPS, and TNF; M2 macrophages by IL-4, IL-13, and IL-33. The M1/M2 paradigm has been questioned as a continuum of states exists, and mixed phenotypes occur in diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C28 provide established background knowledge about macrophage biology, all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

results.result: Prior work established that TPE-FLIM is a label-free, noninvasive imaging method that can distinguish various dermal cell types and functional states. Previous studies showed TPE-FLIM can distinguish macrophages from other dermal cells and ECM, visualize capillaries with distinct signatures, and distinguish functional states of cells including resting vs. activated mast cells in vivo and macrophages ex vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C37 accurately summarize prior work (primarily Kröger et al., 2020 and other cited studies) that provides the foundation for the current study. These claims are well-supported by citations and establish the technical feasibility and rationale for applying TPE-FLIM to macrophage phenotyping.

results.result: IgG stimulation of IgG immune complex-sensitized M1 and M2 macrophages resulted in release of inflammatory mediators but did not lead to significant changes in TPE-FLIM parameters 2 and 5 days after differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 describes an experimental result but explicitly states the data are not shown. Without access to the data, sample sizes, statistical tests, or details of the experimental conditions, this claim cannot be properly evaluated. The result may be valid but requires the supporting data to be assessed.

results.result: The paradigm for macrophage polarization is shifting toward less strict M1/M2 classification. Differences in TPE-FLIM parameters between monocyte-derived and dermal M2 macrophages are attributed to use of different polarization agents (M-CSF + IFN-γ for M1, M-CSF + IL-4 for M2) and microenvironment effects including inflammatory signals, UV exposure, and immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C114, C117-C119 provide interpretation of observed differences in TPE-FLIM parameters between experimental conditions, supported by citations to relevant literature. The explanation is reasonable and acknowledges the complexity of macrophage biology and the limitations of simplified in vitro polarization protocols.

results.result: M2 macrophages are often found in areas of higher density of unknown dermal cells, presumably fibroblasts, compared to M1 macrophages. It is suspected that M2 macrophages in conjunction with collagen-synthesizing fibroblasts are acting toward dermal repair and regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C128 describe an observational pattern but the interpretation is explicitly speculative ("presumably," "suspected"). The identity of the surrounding cells is not confirmed, and the functional relationship is inferred rather than demonstrated. This represents a hypothesis requiring further investigation rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: Technical challenges in ex vivo imaging: M2 macrophages were more difficult to visualize than M1 macrophages in biopsies due to high fluorescence intensity of elastin in dried tissue and decreased signal-to-noise ratio. More CD163+ M2 macrophages were visible in immunohistochemistry compared to TPE-FLIM due to the limited imaging plane of the two-photon tomograph (1.2-2.0 µm) versus thicker biopsy sections (10 µm).
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 provide honest assessment of technical limitations and explain discrepancies between imaging methods. The explanation for differences between TPE-FLIM and immunohistochemistry is logical and supported by the known specifications of the imaging system. This transparency strengthens confidence in the overall findings.

results.result: Skin mast cells stained for tryptase showed a distinct TPE-FLIM signature that distinguished them from M1 and M2 macrophages, confirming previous findings on dermal mast cells in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 provides additional validation that the TPE-FLIM signatures are specific to macrophages by showing mast cells have different signatures. This is supported by imaging data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and citation to previous work (Kröger et al., 2020), strengthening the specificity claims.

results.result: TPE-FLIM parameters within individual macrophages can vary depending on cellular substructures (nucleus, vacuoles, cytoplasm, membrane). Phasor plot analysis shows the relative position of macrophage categories and other cells, with contributions of long and short fluorescence lifetimes.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 describe spatial heterogeneity within cells and the analytical approach. The observations are supported by imaging data (Figure 4a-d) and are consistent with the expected biological complexity of cellular compartments having different metabolic states and thus different fluorescence properties.

results.result: Future research directions: Further investigations are needed to clarify how location, morphology, and function of M1 and M2 macrophages influence their TPE-FLIM parameters in vivo; to characterize the influence of cytoskeletal changes on TPE-FLIM parameters; to assess the impact of age, gender, and disease on macrophage ratio, localization, and function; to investigate the influence of different phagocytosed materials; and to improve the classification approach with depth-adjusted cell size and refined shape parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C140, C148-C149, C166, and C176 appropriately identify limitations and future research directions. These are reasonable suggestions based on the current findings and acknowledged gaps in understanding. They do not represent results but rather appropriate scientific discussion of next steps.

results.result: Morphological and functional characteristics of macrophage phenotypes: M1 macrophages are elongated with dense cortical actin networks and migrate less far than M2 macrophages due to cytoskeletal changes. M2 macrophages are more spherical with randomly distributed actin. Actin reorganization during polarization leads to larger filament bundles reducing cell plasticity. The irregular appearance of M1 macrophages detected by TPE-FLIM is likely a consequence of polarization-specific cytoskeletal changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C147 integrate observations from this study with established literature on macrophage cytoskeletal biology. The interpretations are well-supported by citations and consistent with the imaging data. The connection between cytoskeletal organization and TPE-FLIM appearance is a reasonable inference supported by the literature.

results.result: Study limitations: Long-term in vitro measurements are limited by inability to maintain physiological temperature. Long-term in vivo measurements are limited by difficulty relocating the same cell. The study uses simplified M1/M2 separation without considering mixed phenotypes, which are primarily observed in diseases. Misidentified cells by the decision tree could potentially be mixed phenotype macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C157 provide honest assessment of study limitations. The acknowledgment of the simplified M1/M2 classification is appropriate given the current understanding of macrophage biology. The speculation about misclassified cells potentially being mixed phenotypes is reasonable but explicitly identified as requiring additional experiments.

results.result: Technical considerations for phagocytosis detection: The microenvironment in inflamed skin is acidic (pH<7.35), acidification occurs in phagocytosing macrophages, fluorescence lifetime shifts toward shorter values under acidic conditions, and cells produce ROS under phagocytosis and acidic conditions. TPE-FLIM can potentially detect phagocytosing M1 macrophages but cannot identify what is phagocytized. No internal structure was visible in TPE-FLIM images. Measurement precision could be improved by reducing the instrument response function (<100 ps).
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C169 provide technical context for interpreting phagocytosis-related signals, supported by appropriate citations. The acknowledgment of method limitations (cannot identify phagocytosed material, no internal structure visible) and suggestions for technical improvements demonstrate appropriate scientific rigor.

results.result: Machine learning model characteristics: The decision tree model uses only TPE-FLIM parameters without morphological features, potentially reducing degrees of freedom and saving calculation time. High accuracy for M1 macrophages is attributed to their having the shortest fluorescence lifetimes, highest a1/a2 ratio, and highest fluorescence intensity. M2 macrophages can be misclassified with resting mast cells and in vitro dendritic cells in rare cases. Classification depends only on TPE-FLIM parameters, not morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C174 provide interpretation of the machine learning results. The explanation for M1 classification accuracy is logical given the distinct parameter values. The acknowledgment of potential misclassification with specific cell types is appropriate and suggests areas for refinement. The conclusion that classification is parameter-dependent is supported by the model structure.

results.result: Methods and study design: A two-photon tomograph with femtosecond Ti:sapphire laser was used at 3-5 mW for in vitro/ex vivo and 40-50 mW for in vivo measurements at 760 nm excitation. Band pass filters detected TPE-AF (410-680 nm) and SHG (375-385 nm). Resolution was 1.2-2.0 µm axial and 0.5 µm lateral. Twenty-five healthy volunteers (12 males, 13 females, 24-65 years, skin types I-III) were studied with 6-12 tomograms per subject covering 0.008-0.016 mm³ total volume, with 6.8 s acquisition time per image and ≈30 min per subject, between October 2018 and November 2020.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C191 provide detailed methodological information that is internally consistent and appropriate for the study. The equipment specifications, imaging parameters, and study population are clearly described. The sample size (25 subjects) is reasonable for this type of imaging study, and the imaging volume and time parameters are appropriate.

results.result: Macrophage density in skin biopsies: CD68-stained M1 macrophages showed an average density of 209±25 cells/mm² in papillary dermis and 140±76 cells/mm² in reticular dermis. CD163-stained M2 macrophages showed an average density of 242±126 cells/mm² in papillary dermis and 107±60 cells/mm² in reticular dermis (10 µm cryo-sections).
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C193 provide quantitative data on macrophage density from immunohistochemistry, supported by imaging data (Figures 1c-d). The measurements include appropriate error estimates (standard deviations) and are consistent with the reported density of >100 cells/mm² observed in vivo. The higher variability for M2 cells (larger standard deviations) is noted.

results.result: Table 1 is an extension of results shown in Kröger et al., 2020.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 acknowledges that some data in Table 1 builds on previous work. This is appropriate citation practice and transparency about the relationship between current and prior findings.

results.result: Morphological characteristics in biopsies: CD68-positive dermal M1 macrophages showed heterogeneous appearance ranging from flat spindle-shaped vessel lining to large intravascular cells with irregular borders and nucleus. CD163-positive M2 macrophages showed round to elliptically shaped cells with significantly lower TPE-AF intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 describe morphological observations from combined TPE-FLIM and immunohistochemistry data (Figure 3). The descriptions are consistent with the imaging data and provide additional characterization of the macrophage phenotypes in tissue sections.

results.result: Methodological considerations for in vivo macrophage visualization: Important factors included the preferred localization of macrophages in papillary and reticular dermis, orientation of the focal plane parallel to the skin surface, and need for maximal cellular cross-section visualization requiring high-resolution depth adjustment to reconstruct entire cell structures.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 describes the search strategy developed for in vivo imaging. This methodological approach is logical given the known biology of macrophage localization and the technical constraints of the imaging system. The strategy was successfully applied as demonstrated by the identification of macrophages in vivo.
